claim: The vestibular system encodes motion of the head in space and is vital to our ability to maintain stability during both quiet standing and locomotion.
source: The vestibular system encodes motion of the head in space, and is vital to our ability to maintain stability during both quiet standing and locomotion (Angelaki and Cullen, 2008; Goldberg et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Angelaki and Cullen, 2008 and Goldberg et al., 2012

claim: Vestibular signals influence the activation of muscles engaged in the control of posture.
source: Vestibular signals influence the activation of muscles engaged in the control of posture.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations in the following sentence

claim: The vestibular influence on muscle activation depends on the muscles' active engagement in balance control and the alignment of the muscles' mechanical action with both the plane of instability and the direction of the vestibular disturbance.
source: This influence depends on the muscles' active engagement in balance control, and the alignment of the muscles' mechanical action with both the plane of instability and the direction of the vestibular disturbance (Lund and Broberg, 1983; Britton et al., 1993; Fitzpatrick et al., 1994; Luu et al., 2012; Mian and Day, 2014; Forbes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies from 1983 to 2016

claim: Contextually-dependent vestibular responses have been observed during both quiet standing and locomotion.
source: Contextually-dependent vestibular responses have been observed during both quiet standing (Lund and Broberg, 1983; Fitzpatrick et al., 1994; Marsden et al., 2002; Son et al., 2008; Luu et al., 2012; Mian and Day, 2014; Forbes et al., 2016) and locomotion, where the magnitude of vestibular-evoked muscle responses are modulated further during the phase of the gait cycle (Orlovsky, 1972; Matsuyama and Drew, 2000; Blouin et al., 2011; Dakin et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations for both quiet standing and locomotion contexts

claim: The magnitude of vestibular-evoked muscle responses are modulated during the phase of the gait cycle during locomotion.
source: Contextually-dependent vestibular responses have been observed during both quiet standing (Lund and Broberg, 1983; Fitzpatrick et al., 1994; Marsden et al., 2002; Son et al., 2008; Luu et al., 2012; Mian and Day, 2014; Forbes et al., 2016) and locomotion, where the magnitude of vestibular-evoked muscle responses are modulated further during the phase of the gait cycle (Orlovsky, 1972; Matsuyama and Drew, 2000; Blouin et al., 2011; Dakin et al., 2013; Forbes et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on gait cycle modulation

claim: Ten healthy young males completed the locomotor transition experiment.
source: In the first study, ten healthy young males completed two blocks of 105 trials where they were instructed to stand quietly, then initiate locomotion, walking at their preferred speed for ~3.5 m, and then to turn around and walk back to their initial position where they were instructed to stand quietly again (defined as the 'locomotor transition' experiment).
evidence: Direct statement about the study participants and design

claim: Participants performed one block with the head facing forward and another block with the head turned 90° over the left shoulder.
source: Participants performed one block with the head facing forward and another block with the head turned 90° over the left shoulder (Figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement about experimental conditions with reference to Figure 1

claim: Participants received 30 s of non-painful electrical vestibular stimulus (EVS) behind the ears during each trial.
source: Participants received 30 s of a non-painful electrical vestibular stimulus (EVS) behind the ears (Materials and methods) which lasted the duration of each trial.
evidence: Direct statement about the experimental stimulus

claim: Six additional subjects completed the posture-to-posture transition experiment.
source: In the second study, six additional subjects (young adults, three females) completed one block of 105 trials where they were instructed to stand quietly, then shift their body-weight laterally to redistribute their weight so that 90% was supported by their preferred leg and only 10% by their non-preferred leg (defined as the 'posture-to-posture transition' experiment).
evidence: Direct statement about the second study participants and design

claim: During quiet standing preceding locomotion onset, subjects swayed generating low amplitude shear forces at the feet with a root-mean-square of 0.39 ± 0.3 N.
source: During the quiet standing period preceding the onset of locomotion, subjects swayed, generating low amplitude shear forces at the feet (root-mean-square of 0.39 ± 0.3 N) and relatively small accelerations of the head (averaged horizontal linear acceleration <0.01 ± 0.3 m/s2) (Figure 2).

claim: During quiet standing preceding locomotion onset, subjects exhibited relatively small accelerations of the head with averaged horizontal linear acceleration <0.01 ± 0.3 m/s2.
